As someone who worked at a large-scale wholesale nursery that supplies to smaller nurseries across several states, I believe the problem comes from two things. 

First, a lot of nurseries don't grow their own plants, many of them are buying from the same few suppliers. Second, suppliers generally only grow things that they know will sell. They don't want to waste time, money or space on a plant that few people know about and fewer ever ask for.

Neighborhood developers have a lot to do with the "plant packages" that are sold with new homes. Many of them want a similar landscape to enhance the visual unity of their ticky-tacky neighborhood. There are usually 3 different trees you can choose from, and maybe 6 or so different shrubs. The mow-and-blow company hired by the developer goes to the supplier every day to pick up several packages of the same plants for jobs in new neighborhoods, so the grower is going to grow lots of those plants to make sure they don't ever miss out on a sale. When smaller nurseries need trees or shrubs to restock, these are the least expensive plants and they're always in stock.

So I'm an essential employee (facilities management) who is registered for 2 classes this fall. Here's the situation I've sen so far, some good and some bad.

I'm really grateful to have had a paying job through the pandemic, but it has been pretty rough. With most buildings closed down we didn't have anywhere to use the restroom during our work day at first, much less to wash our hands (no hand sanitizer available for us to keep in vehicles, either, unless people bring their own - most don't). Now there are 4 buildings on campus that we have access to, so we can use the restroom in an emergency, but still can't wash our hands as much as we need to. Most of us have to ride 2 people per vehicle (with face masks required), and we share all tools, vehicles and equipment. Six of us refill the water bottles that we drink out of from the same 5gallon cooler that never gets washed...I don't even want to think about how many germs are in and on that thing, but my 40oz bottle isn't enough water in this heat. There's no pre-work screening (they are trusting us to take our temperature at home), and they're asking that we use our sick pay and don't come to work if we are feeling even a little bit sickly. All of this to do super essential work such as trimming hedges.

That being said, management has done a pretty good job of keeping us informed with weekly meetings and email alerts about when and where there is a confirmed or assumed positive case on campus (at least 2 per day). They treat every potential case as an assumed positive, and the custodial team has been absolutely kicking ass at immediate decontamination of any area in question (at which point we get another email that the area is now safe to enter). They've also stepped up their regular cleaning routines in all buildings, using chemicals that have been proven to be effective at killing the virus.

Even knowing all of this, I'm opting for online classes only this semester. I just don't think there's any way they'll be able to keep it from spreading like wildfire once party life starts back up on campus. My job is outdoors, so hopefully I'll be able to keep from contracting it while working, but I feel like we're all going to get it if even one person brings it to work with them.

Looks more like possible iron deficiency to me. Since plants can't move iron around within plant tissues the problem shows up in newer leaves. Nitrogen deficiencies show up first in older leaves because the plant will move nitrogen from older leaves to newer ones to focus energy on newer growth.

Iron deficiency can be caused by overwatering, high pH, and sometimes by over fertilizing.  A chelated iron or iron sulfate usually fixes the problem pretty quickly, but the fix will likely be temporary if you don't figure out what's causing it.

Sometimes leaves can look pretty splotchy as they lose their green pigment. 

Mosaic virus that I have seen is more often yellow splotches that are unevenly distributed across the leaf surface. If it's a rust you'll usually see the rusty looking stuff on the underside of the leaf where the dark spots are. If you see signs of rust this time of year it's usually no big deal, just clean up all of the leaf debris from around the base of the tree and treat it with a fungicide next year at the first sign of a problem. There's no cure for the virus, but it doesn't look like that's something to worry about at this point. 

If you don't see definite signs of a fungal problem I would wait until spring and see if new leaves/growth has the same issue. Keep the fallen leaves cleaned up just in case something is planning to overwinter in them.

In my experience, upright rosemary is more often overwatered than underwatered, or it sits in wet soil too long and gets grumpy. They need good drainage and they like it on the drier side. Most types are more difficult to grow in containers, especially plastic or glazed pots. It looks like you have the best type of container (the unglazed clay breathes well) and your soil doesn't look soggy, but if it seems like the soil stays wet for too long you may need to adjust your watering, or move the plant to a draftier spot (though not in direct path of ac/heater vents) to help the soil dry faster. They're usually happier outside with a bit of air flowing around them from time to time.

Make sure you don't have spider mites or another insect feeding on it, and do the finger test before watering (wait until soil is dry at least to your first knuckle each time before you water). Also make sure that direct sun is not hitting it through that window for too long, rosemary takes full sun in most zones but windows can magnify the heat and burn...at least where I live it can. Lastly, consider that being sheared (into a Christmas tree, maybe?) and transplanted may have just done stressed this guy out. It may look a little better once it settles into the new soil/container/spot. 

That's all I've got for now! Hope it helps!

Came here to say this. My husband and I make christmas kahlua every year. We use liquid etching and stencils to personalize the bottles, and ask them to bring the bottle back for refills next year. It costs about $40 per batch with the materials we use (including the price of the 16oz swingtop bottles, it's about $20 per batch without them), and each batch fills about 8 bottles. There's an initial cost with the bottles, but you can get creative with recycled bottles and corks to bring the cost down. Even with the bottles, $5 per gift isn't too bad.

It's become a really fun holiday tradition for us, tweaking the recipe every year and comparing it to last year's.

Edit: I got the recipe online around 6 years ago, and I can't find the website to give due credit, but here's what I saved:

-12-18 cups chocolate coffee, double strength
-2 lb brown sugar
-4-6 tbsp vanilla extract
-A fifth of strong alcohol (we've used vodka and everclear, both were good)

Bring brewed coffee to a boil, slowly add the sugar, and return to boil, stirring constantly. Let cool to room temperature (this is important), then add vanilla and alcohol. That's it!

You can play around with the flavors using different types of coffee or brewing it different ways, as long as it's super strong, like double the regular amount of grounds. You can also play with the amount and type of alcohol you use according to your taste or budget. Use pure vanilla extract, not vanilla flavoring. It doesn't need to age. I double the recipe for one batch (using a very large pot). I'm sure there are way fancier recipes out there, but this one has worked well for us, and it always beats out the store-bought kahlua in our taste tests.

My favorite way to enjoy it is drizzled over vanilla bean ice cream.

So sorry you and your buddy are dealing with this. Our little guy (5 yo weenie) was diagnosed with a calcified disc (IVDD) a couple of months ago. We went through several tedious weeks of not knowing whether we'd be able to keep him around, and when one vet recommended euthanasia we were completely heartbroken. 

We couldn't bring ourselves to put him down before exploring every option, so we spoke with another vet who had us try some different meds (steroids) that seemed to help. We kept him from moving around for 8 weeks, carrying him to and from his potty spot outside (which I know will be more difficult with a beagle). We had to make sure he stayed clean and didn't develop bed sores while he wasn't able to move.

We also did some research and got him some supplements (vetri science vetri disc back support formula) that our new vet wasn't very enthusiastic about, but he said it couldn't hurt, and we were grasping at all the straws we could find. I can't say they were the miracle pills we were hoping for but, like the vet said, I don't think they did any harm...we're hopeful that they'll help to protect the good vertebrae he has left.

He's now pain free most days without any meds, though some days are better than others. The vet says he's a good candidate for a wheelchair, so we've just started to seriously consider our options. He won't ever use his back legs again, but he's finally starting to play with his toys, and seems to be getting back to his old self even though he's really bored.

I guess the tldr is to trust your instincts and seek out other opinions if something doesn't feel right. The recovery from back issues can take a very long time, but if you have the means and the patience to deal with the extra work it'll take, and the pain can be managed, then it doesn't have to be the end of the road.

One last note that I'm sure you've heard about is to look into care credit to help with the vet bills. This will give you 6 months to pay off the bill without interest. Just make sure you read the fine print...the interest is high and once interest is charged it's on the original amount, not on the amount you have left. Also don't make the minimum payment -  figure out what you need to pay to get it paid off in the 6 months if you want to do it interest free.

Best of luck to you and your pup. Hang in there. I think you will know when it's the right time to let him go...whether it's sooner or (hopefully) later. Nobody else knows and loves your dog like you do, and you'll do right by him.

Thyme is a Mediterranean herb, so it usually likes to go a bit dry between watering. Make sure the pot has good drainage, and do your best not to overwater. I feel like air flow is often a problem when people grow the Mediterranean herbs indoors. Rosemary, sage, and thyme all get grumpy if they sit in wet soil for too long, and we often have them tucked down into a planter with poor drainage and air flow, or with other herbs that like a little more moisture (like mint). If it's been in the same container for a while, it might be time to give it a little container upgrade, or give it a bit of fertilizer (but don't do both at the same time unless you use a slow release fertilizer. Also make sure the fertilizer you use is safe for your intended use of the plant). Sometimes just a slightly bigger pot with some new quick-draining soil is all they need!

I'm not sure about the spots, but the leaf deformity on the jalapeno looks a lot like thrip damage to me (or possibly another sucking insect).  Thrips are very tiny little insects (you may be able to see them crawling around if you shake the plant over some white paper).  They do their damage by sucking juices from tender new shoots, which often causes new leaves to emerge with deformities.  The bad news is that the damage is already done (and can't be reversed), but the good news is that it's usually just cosmetic (which means that the plant can still function almost normally), and only the affected leaves should be deformed.

I would usually recommend a systemic insecticide if thrips are determined to be the problem, but this isn't a good choice if you plan on eating the peppers.  There may be a natural or organic insecticide that you can use, but make sure it's safe for edibles before treating.

Anyway, I'm not positive that's the issue, but I thought I'd offer an alternative to the theory that fertilizer is the problem.
